creative.description:
I've been a musculoskeletal pain specialist for 22 years and if your hands have been getting stiffer, achier, and harder to use…

Then what I am about to share with you is going to OUTRAGE you.

My name is Dr. Sarah. Board-certified musculoskeletal pain specialist.

Twenty-two years treating chronic joint pain, osteoarthritis, and the kind of hand and finger pain that slowly steals your independence one small task at a time.

And I'm breaking ranks with my own profession to tell you this.

So let me tell you what happened with one of my patients because her story is going to open your eyes to how messed up this really is.

Her name was Linda. 58 years old.

For four straight years, she dealt with this.

Her fingers so stiff in the morning they curled up tightly and were hard to open. By lunchtime her knuckles were aching. By evening she could barely grip a kettle. She had been active her whole life, knitted jumpers for her grandchildren, gardened every weekend, opened every jar in the house without thinking, and suddenly she had the hands of someone twenty years older.

She came through my clinic. Multiple doctors. Her GP. A physiotherapist. A rheumatologist. Me, the pain specialist. Thousands of pounds in appointments, blood tests, X-rays, referrals.

And you know what every single one of us told her?

"Your bloods are normal. It's not rheumatoid."

"It's just osteoarthritis. Wear and tear. Normal for your age."

"Take ibuprofen."

"Wear compression gloves."

Wear compression gloves. This woman couldn't open a jar of horseradish and we were telling her to buy tighter gloves.

Then we put her on naproxen. Then Voltarol gel three times a day. Then cortisone injections into her finger joints.

You know what happened?

The naproxen gave her stomach cramps so bad she stopped eating breakfast. The Voltarol wore off in an hour. The cortisone worked for six weeks, then four, then barely two.

And her hands? Still stiff. Still aching. Still getting worse.

The treatments masked the pain. But the joints kept degrading. The stiffness kept spreading. The life kept shrinking.

I watched this woman do everything I told her, spend thousands of pounds, take my prescriptions, and get worse. Not better. Worse.

And I did not understand why.

Until an integrative pain researcher stopped me in my tracks at a conference and taught me more about stiff, aching hands in thirty minutes than I had learned in two decades of practice.

November 2023. Edinburgh. The British Pain Society annual meeting.

I was sitting at a table during a coffee break, trying to uncurl my own fingers around the cup without wincing. Because eighteen months earlier — right around the time I went through the menopause — my own hands had started stiffening. And nothing I had been prescribing to patients for twenty-two years was working on me either.

That is when I noticed him.

Dr. Michael Lin. Integrative pain and inflammation researcher. He'd been writing notes all morning. Picking up his coffee. Shaking hands with colleagues. His fingers moved the way fingers move when they have never once been thought about.

No stiffness. No swollen knuckles. No hesitation before gripping.

I walked over.

"Excuse me. At your age, after writing all morning, how are your hands not in bits?"

He smiled.

The kind of smile that knows something you don't.

Then he looked down at my hands.

He didn't need to ask what was wrong.

"Dr. Sarah, may I show you something?"

"It'll take thirty minutes."

"But it'll completely change the way you understand hand and finger pain."

He pulled out a notepad.

Then he wrote one sentence across the top:

Joint degeneration is a symptom, NOT the root cause.

I stared at the words.

Because for nearly two decades, I'd been taught to treat stiff, aching hands as a joint problem.

Mask the pain with anti-inflammatories.

Rub on topical gel.

Squeeze the swelling down with compression gloves.

Inject cortisone into the worst joints.

And when all of that fails, tell the patient it's something they'll have to learn to live with.

But nobody had explained why the joints were breaking down to begin with.

Then the doctor said something I'd never heard before.

"The question you should be asking isn't…"

"'How do I stop the pain in the hands?'"

"The real question should be…"

"'Why are the joints in her fingers and wrists breaking down faster than her body can repair them?'"

That sentence hit me like a brick.

Because every treatment I'd prescribed worked the same way.

Painkillers masked the pain signal.

Voltarol gel temporarily numbed the surface.

Compression gloves squeezed the swelling.

Cortisone injections temporarily suppressed the local inflammation.

But none of them addressed why the inflammation was there in the first place.

He drew a simple picture of a finger joint.

Then he drew tiny arrows flooding in around the cartilage.

"This is chronic low-grade inflammation," he said.

"After menopause, a woman's body loses oestrogen."

"Oestrogen is the body's most powerful natural anti-inflammatory."

"Losing it is like removing a brake."

"Without that brake, inflammatory signals begin flooding the joints — especially the small, delicate joints in the hands and fingers."

Then he tapped the drawing.

"The inflammation attacks the cartilage. The cartilage thins. The joints stiffen. The fingers curl. The grip goes. The pain gets worse."

"And every treatment you prescribe treats what happens AFTER the inflammation has already done its damage."

Then he drew a tap above the hand with water pouring down.

"That's like mopping up a flooded floor while the tap is still running."

"You're cleaning up the damage."

"Not turning off what's causing it."

I sat there thinking about every patient I'd put on naproxen.

Every patient I'd told to buy compression gloves.

Every patient I'd injected with cortisone.

Every patient I'd told there was nothing more I could do.

I'd been treating the damage after it happened.

I hadn't been helping the body turn down the inflammation that was causing the damage in the first place.

Then he said something else I'd never heard in medical school.

"As women get older — especially after menopause — the inflammation becomes harder for the body to shut off on its own."

"Without oestrogen's protective brake, it accumulates."

"And as the chronic inflammation builds up around the finger joints, the wrists, the surrounding tissue…"

"The joints degrade faster than the body can repair them."

"When you're younger, your body can usually manage the inflammation and maintain the joint."

"But after 50, that balance shifts."

"The inflammation makes the small joints in the hands more vulnerable to breakdown."

"That's why temporarily masking the pain isn't the same as supporting a healthy inflammatory response."

This was the missing piece.

Because joint degeneration wasn't the root cause.

It was the symptom.

And for many women over 50 with stiff, aching, swollen hands, chronic post-menopausal inflammation was the hidden problem nobody was talking about.

Then he turned the page.

"Fortunately, there's one little-known pressure point most women over 50 are missing in this conversation."

I leaned forward.

He said:

"There's a point that runs along the index finger down to the webbing between the thumb. Healers call it the Hegu point. LI-4."

"It's been documented for over four thousand years."

"The Yellow Emperor's texts describe it. Modern acupuncturists still use it. Memorial Sloan Kettering teaches it."

"For four thousand years, stimulating this one point on the hand has been used to help the body calm its own pain and inflammatory signals."

"And here's what makes it so relevant for hand pain specifically."

He tapped the drawing of the hand.

"The Hegu point is ON the hand. The pressure point that helps regulate inflammation sits in the exact same area as the joints that are being damaged by it."

This was the missing piece.

And once you understand what consistent stimulation at this pressure point does…

You may never look at painkillers, compression gloves, and cortisone injections the same way again.

Because this one pressure point helps support healthy circulation through the hands and fingers.

It helps support the body's own pain-regulation pathways.

It helps support a healthier inflammation response — helping the body turn down the chronic inflammatory signals that are driving the joint damage.

And ultimately, it helps support what every painkiller, gel, glove, and injection fails to do — address the inflammation itself, not just the pain it causes.

I'd been treating the damaged joints.

But I hadn't been supporting the system responsible for protecting them.

Every treatment I'd prescribed for twenty-two years worked downstream.

Not one of them addressed the chronic inflammation attacking the joints from the inside.

And here's what made my blood boil.

This pressure point has been documented for four thousand years. Acupuncturists use it every single day. Researchers have studied it in clinical settings across the world.

But the connection between this pressure point, chronic inflammation, and hand pain after menopause was almost never discussed in mainstream medicine.

A small British company has now designed a ring — a simple, beautiful ring with therapeutic magnets — that delivers gentle, consistent acupressure stimulation at the Hegu point.

You wear it on the hand that needs it most. Every day.

And instead of masking the pain signal or numbing the surface or squeezing the swelling or injecting cortisone that wears off in a fortnight…

It helps the body turn down the tap.

Week 5. I took it off to prove Dot wrong, the same way she had. By day four I was stiff again and back on the settee by three. I put it back on, and it hasn't left my finger since.

Week 6. Three o'clock came and went, and I didn't sit down. I didn't even notice until tea.

Week 7. I got down on the floor with my grandson's Lego, and I got back up by myself.

Week 8. I took the walking stick out of the umbrella stand and walked the three-mile loop round the reservoir. The next morning, I did it again.

Week 10. My sister met me for lunch and stopped dead in the doorway of the café. "Janet. What are you taking?"

Week 12. I packed my suitcase. My good jeans needed a belt. Half a stone.

The ring didn't walk that half stone off me. I did. It just gave me back a body that wanted to move.

That's what doing nothing looks like, by the way.

On the Saturday of half-term, I got a taxi to Manchester Airport by myself.

Chloe had no idea I was coming.

She found out at the hotel pool on the Sunday afternoon. She was walking past with two women from her office, and she stopped so fast one of them walked into the back of her.

"Jan? What are you doing here?"

Doing nothing, I said. Like you told me.

On the Tuesday the whole team went on a day trip up into the mountains. Nobody had invited me. I'd put my name down at reception the day I arrived, and I was the first one on the coach.

It was the Caminito del Rey. They used to call it the most dangerous path in the world. A narrow walkway bolted to the side of a gorge, a hundred metres of nothing underneath, and a swaying bridge at the very end.

At the start, the guide asked if anybody wanted to stay with the coach and mind the bags.

I picked up my walking stick and set off.

Now go, Jan.

I was standing in the middle of that bridge when the group caught up. A young lad from Chloe's office came over with his hands on his knees, puffing.

"Sorry, I've got to ask. How old are you?"

63, I said.

"My mum's 58 and she can't do her own stairs. What are you on?"

Chloe was right behind him. She heard every word.

And when we got back to the start, there was one person sitting on the bench by the coach, minding everybody's bags.

Chloe. She'd turned her ankle on the stony path down to the start and come back to wait, with a bag of ice from the cool box on her foot.

I took one picture. Just one.

I've never posted it.

On the Friday night the hotel put on a flamenco night. When the dancers came round pulling people up, they pulled me, in front of Chloe's entire office, and I danced the whole song.

When I sat back down, a woman about my age leaned over from the next table.

"I'm sorry, I have to ask. I've watched you all week. What's your secret?"

I held up my hand. I told her about Dot and the late slip, and about the four little magnets and the clock.

Chloe was three seats down. She put her fork down and didn't pick it up again.

That night she knocked on my door.

No make-up. Hair in a clip. Her ankle wrapped in a tea towel full of ice from the bar.

She sat down in the other chair on my balcony, and for a long time she didn't say anything.

"I put that picture on the family WhatsApp," she said finally.

You did.

"I've been telling everyone for two years that you can't keep up. That you just sit." She looked at her ankle. "And this week I'm the one who sat on a bench minding everybody's bags."

I let that sit.

"Everybody always talks about how you brought Mark up on your own. How you did everything. I've got three kids and a full-time job and I'm drowning, Jan. It was easier if you were the one who couldn't."

"I said you don't do anything anymore. That was a horrible thing to say."

It was the first thing she'd ever said to me that didn't have a smile on top of it.

Then she looked at my hand.

"Where do I get one? Not for me. For my mum. She's 61, and I haven't invited her anywhere in three years because I thought she'd slow us down."

I told her to leave her mother to me.

And then I told her something I hadn't planned to say. If she ever needed me to have the kids for a weekend, I would. Not because I don't do anything anymore. Because I want to.

She cried. A proper cry, the first I'd ever seen from her.

I changed the Netflix password back the next morning.

My son rang that afternoon. She'd told him everything.

"Mum. That picture. I'm so sorry. I should have said something years ago."

I know, love.

Chloe rang me again last week, to ask what time she should drop the kids off. Right before she hung up, she said, "Thanks, Mum."

Twelve years. First time.

Somewhere over the Bay of Biscay on the way home, I worked out what that autumn had really been about.

For 34 years I looked after everybody. Then my body slowed down, and the people I'd looked after decided I was the one who needed looking after.

And the worst part is, I half believed them.

I wasn't old. My clock was running slow, and in 63 years nobody had ever told me why.

creative.description:
My ex-husband rang to say he was bringing his 29-year-old girlfriend to our daughter's wedding. "Stand at the back, Jan. You stopped taking care of yourself." I smiled, hung up, and spent twelve weeks showing him what taking care of myself looks like.

I've taught at Hillgate Primary in Stockport for 26 years. Year 3, mostly, with a spell in Year 6 I try not to think about. Last spring my daughter Emma's boyfriend, Jake, proposed to her in my kitchen, next to the kettle.

He'd asked me first. That night he gave me the very first invitation, before anybody else had one. On the back he'd written three words in biro.

Front row, Jan.

I stuck it on the fridge with a magnet from Blackpool. Remember that it's there.

Three weeks later I was at the kitchen table with a brew and the seating plan when my phone lit up with Steve's name.

In three years, Steve has never once rung to ask how I am. He only rings when he wants something.

He didn't say hello.

"Jan, I'm bringing Kayleigh to the wedding. She's part of my life now. You need to accept that."

Then, before I could answer:

"And do yourself a favour. Stand at the back. You stopped taking care of yourself a long time ago."

I told him I'd been thinking about the front row, actually.

He laughed. Not a nasty laugh, exactly. Worse. The kind of laugh you'd give a child who says she's going to be an astronaut.

"Front row? Jan. Have you looked in a mirror lately? Those photos are going on Emma's wall forever. Do her a favour and stand at the back."

I said Emma had asked him not to bring her. He said Emma would get over it.

So I smiled, which he couldn't see, and I said, I'll see you at the wedding, Steve. And I hung up.

I had never hung up on anyone in my life.

Emma rang him that night, on speaker, with Jake sat next to her. "If she comes, you don't."

"Don't be dramatic, Em," he said. Then, after a long gap, "Fine. I won't bring her. I promise."

She believed him. So did I. That was our mistake.

I need to tell you about the day he left.

It was a Tuesday in November, three years ago. I'd made shepherd's pie. Steve came in, didn't take his coat off, and stood by the back door with his car keys in his hand.

"Look at you, Jan. You don't look like the woman I married. You stopped taking care of yourself. I'm just not attracted to you anymore. That's the truth."

Thirty years. He said it in about fifteen seconds.

Then he went out to the car. It was chucking it down. Kayleigh was already in the passenger seat with the heater on.

I stood at the counter with the oven gloves still on. The shepherd's pie stayed in the oven until Thursday.

An hour after I hung up on him, my phone started buzzing with Facebook. Kayleigh had posted a photo of the two of them on a balcony in Tenerife. Cocktails, matching sunglasses.

"Some of us got the upgrade 😂"

Then a second photo.

It was me. At my niece's christening, two years ago. Grey cardigan, hair scraped back, eating a sausage roll at the buffet with my eyes half shut.

She'd put it right next to her own.

Fourteen people liked it.

One of them was my son.

I'm not proud of what I did next. I went into WhatsApp and blocked Steve. Thirty years of the same number, gone with one press of my thumb.

It felt wonderful for about four minutes.

Then I went upstairs to try on dresses for the wedding.

There were six on the bed, three on the carpet, and one stuck halfway over my shoulders that I couldn't get up or down. I sat on my bedroom floor with my arms over my head and looked at myself in the wardrobe mirror for a long, long time.

The woman in the mirror. Grey roots. Puffy face. The same cardigan on the chair behind her that she'd worn all week.

Because the part I'd never said out loud was that Steve wasn't wrong.

I'm 58, and somewhere in those three years I'd stopped recognising myself. I woke up every morning crippled, crumpled and generally knackered. I went up my own stairs one at a time, holding the rail. My clothes had gone tight and my face had gone puffy, and I couldn't tell you how.

I was wiped out by three in the afternoon and wide awake at three in the morning. I'd stopped going to Zumba with my sister Sue. I did my big shop at ten o'clock at night so I wouldn't bump into anyone I knew. I didn't want anybody seeing what I'd turned into.

I'd started saying "you lot go, I'll stay here with the dog" so often that people stopped asking.

And it wasn't for lack of trying. Retinol, collagen, diet shakes. A gym I went to until everything ached so much I quit. Turmeric for the aches. Paracetamol and ibuprofen that didn't touch the sides. Hundreds of pounds. My GP gave me eight minutes. "It's your age, Jan. Take paracetamol and try to get out more."

So maybe Steve had it right. Maybe this was who I was now. The woman who stopped taking care of herself.

That Sunday Emma and Jake came round for tea with the photographer's list.

"I'm not going to be in the photos, love," I said. "Do them with Jake's family. I'll stand at the back."

Jake put his mug down. "There are no photos without you in them, Jan. I'll cancel the photographer first."

Then I looked over at the fridge.

Front row, Jan.

I got my phone out and booked a fitting with Rosa Bennett, who does alterations from her front room on Hillcrest Road. A proper mother-of-the-bride dress. Twelve weeks before the wedding.

Then I sat back in my chair and my hands started shaking, because I'd just told Steve I'd see him at the front, and I couldn't get a zip past my own shoulders.

The next Saturday Emma took me to the Trafford Centre to find a dress.

We did four shops. In the third one, the girl on the changing rooms looked at me in a navy dress with the zip open at the back and said, "We do a lovely bolero jacket, for ladies who'd rather cover up."

I bought the bolero.

In the car park I sat in the driver's seat for ten minutes before I started the engine. I kept turning my wedding ring round and round. Three years, and I'd never taken it off.

Eleven weeks and six days.

Rosa ran the office at Hillgate for 31 years before she retired. She was the one who showed me where the staffroom kettle was on my first day, and she still knows every child's name and every teacher's secret.

I almost cancelled. I'm glad I didn't.

Rosa didn't sit down once. She was up a stepladder getting a roll of satin off the top shelf. Then she was down on the carpet on both knees, pinning a hem for the bride before me. Then she was back up again, without putting a hand on anything, and I watched her do it like I was watching a magic trick.

Then she did it again, because she'd dropped a pin.

She's 13 years older than me. If I'd gone down on that carpet, it would have taken Emma and Rosa both to get me back up.

"Mother of the bride," Rosa said. "Up on the box. Let's see the dress."

I stood on the box in the navy dress with the bolero over it. "Can you just let it out? I'll keep the jacket on."

Rosa took the jacket off me and hung it on the door.

So when she came back with her pin cushion, I asked her straight out. "Rosa, how old are you now?"

"71," she said. "71 in March."

Emma said "71?" out loud before she could stop herself.

"I'm 58," I said, "and I can't look at myself in that mirror. How on earth are you doing all that?"

She laughed so hard she had to put her pin cushion down.

"Love, at 65 I couldn't get off my own settee without rocking three times. My daughter was pricing up stairlifts. I was about this close to letting her."

Then she held up her right hand. A slim gold ring, worn soft at the edges.

"My sister put this on me. She's 84 and still drives herself to Cornwall every Easter. I wore it to shut her up."

I told her I'd seen better rings in a Christmas cracker.

"So did I," she said. "So I took it off for a week to prove her wrong. By Thursday I was back on that settee, rocking."

Then she explained it the way Rosa explains everything, like you're a supply teacher about to be late for registration.

"Your blood runs through little tubes, Jan. When you're young they're soft and stretchy. After fifty they stiffen up, like an old garden hose left out all winter. So the blood slows down, and everything it feeds goes stiff and heavy and tired."

"You remember the master clock in my office? The one that rang every bell in the building? When that clock ran slow, the whole school went haywire. Kids late for dinner, playtime running over, coaches sat in the car park, and every teacher in the building blaming every other teacher. It was never the teachers. It was one clock."

"Your knees, your back, your sleep, the three o'clock slump. You don't have five problems, love. You've got one clock running slow."

I thought about my kitchen cupboard. All those bottles. Every one of them for a different teacher.

"And this," she said, tapping her hand, "is the office."

She took my hand and pressed the back of my finger, just below the knuckle. "Healers have been pressing points on the fingers for thousands of years to ease pain somewhere else entirely. There's four little magnets on the inside of this ring, sat right on those points. They send a pulse into the blood vessels, all day and all night. Softens them up. Gets the blood moving. Puts the clock back on time."

Then she pointed at me in the mirror.

"Blood starts moving again, and everything follows. The aches go, so you move. You move, so the weight comes off. You sleep, and your face, Jan. The colour comes back."

I asked why I couldn't just press it myself.

"You'd have to sit there pressing it all day. This does it while you're asleep."

Then why had no doctor ever said a single word about it?

"Eight minutes, Jan. They haven't got time to tell you about your own blood."

And then the question I was actually scared to ask. Is this going to get me to that front row?

"No," she said. "Your legs are. This just gets the blood back to them."

I already had my phone out, looking at the £9.99 ones on Amazon. She took it right out of my hand.

"Not those. Two weak magnets in a band that turns you green, and you take it off at bedtime. That's why everybody thinks it's a gimmick. Off is no good, Jan. The minute it's off, the clock slows down again."

Then she reached into her sewing box, took out a pad of old Hillgate late slips that she apparently still keeps, and wrote a name on the back of one.

EverCalm.

"Get the gold one. It'll go with the navy. When's the wedding?"

Eleven weeks on Saturday.

"Then order it tonight, and come back in ten weeks for your final fitting. And Jan? Don't you dare tell him."

I ordered it sat outside on Hillcrest Road, before I'd even put my seatbelt on.

Week 1. Nothing at all. I texted Rosa that I wanted my late slip back.

Week 2. I slept through the night. I woke up at seven and checked the clock twice.

Week 3. I came down the stairs, put the kettle on, and I was pouring the milk before I noticed I hadn't touched the rail. I went to the hall mirror. My face wasn't puffy.

Week 5. I left it by the sink at Jake's parents' in Cornwall. By day four I was puffy and aching again and back on the settee by three. I drove two hours down the A30 to get it back, and it hasn't left my finger since.

Week 6. I went back to Zumba with Sue. I stood at the back. By the end I'd moved to the front.

Week 7. Jake came round to fix my shower and stopped dead in the hall. "Jan? What? You look great."

Week 8. I walked the three-mile loop round Reddish Vale with the dog. The next morning, I did it again.

Week 10. The final fitting. Rosa took the dress in two inches at the waist. "Two inches," she said. "I told you."

Week 12. I took my wedding ring off and put it in my handbag. I gave the bolero to the charity shop.

The ring didn't walk those two inches off me. I did. It just gave me back a body that wanted to move.

That's what "stopped taking care of herself" looks like, by the way.

On the morning of the wedding I was in the church porch with Sue, about to go in and take my seat.

The wedding car pulled up at the gate. Steve got out, then Emma, in her dress.

Kayleigh was waiting for him by the gate. She'd come in a taxi.

Emma saw her before I did.

"You promised me you wouldn't bring her."

"Don't do this today, sweetheart."

My daughter slapped her father across the face, right there on the path. Then she said it again, quieter. "You promised me."

Then I stepped out of the porch.

He expected to find me the way he'd left me. Heavier, greyer, hiding in a cardigan.

His jaw dropped. Kayleigh had to say his name twice.

"Jan? What've you done?"

Taken care of myself, I said. Like you told me.

I walked straight past him, all the way down the aisle, and I sat down.

Front row, Jan.

He walked Emma down that aisle, and she told me afterwards he stared at the back of my head the whole way instead of at her.

At the front, Jake leaned over to her and whispered, "Look at your mum."

Steve missed all of it.

After the service the photographer lined us all up on the church steps. He looked at the group and said, "Can somebody stand at the back and mind the bags?"

And there was one person stood at the back, holding everybody's handbags.

Kayleigh. Nobody had asked her to be in a single photo.

I took one picture of her on my phone. Just one.

I've never posted it.

At the evening do, Jake came over to my table. "Jan, will you dance with me?"

Halfway through the song, Steve tapped him on the shoulder. "Mind if I cut in?"

Jake didn't even look at him. "Actually, I do."

When I sat back down, Sue's friend Pauline leaned over from the next table. "Jan! You look ten years younger! What are you doing?"

I held up my hand. "Magnets and pressure points. It's a ring from EverCalm."

"Spell it."

Steve was three seats down. He put his pint down and didn't pick it up again.

Later he found me outside by the smoking shelter. No jacket. Tie undone. A red mark still on his cheek.

He stood there for a long time and didn't say anything.

"I told everybody for three years you'd let yourself go." He looked down at his shirt, straining over his belt. "Then I saw you at that church, and I caught myself in the window of the wedding car. Grey. Red in the face. Out of breath from the steps. I'm the one who's let himself go, Jan."

I let that sit.

"Everybody always says you held that family together. You did everything. I was fifty-five and frightened of getting old. It was easier to say it was you than look at myself."

"What I said in that kitchen. That was a horrible thing to say."

It was the first thing he'd ever said to me without a smirk on top of it.

I opened my handbag and gave him back his wedding ring. Then I told him something I hadn't planned to say. Emma wanted one photo of the three of us. Just one. Not for him. For her.

In the ladies' afterwards, Kayleigh was at the mirror. She watched me in the glass for a long time.

"Can I ask where you got it? Not for me. For my mum. She's 55, and she won't leave the house."

I told her to leave her mother to me.

I unblocked Steve the next morning and sent him the photo of the three of us.

At the end of the night Emma found me on the bench outside, with my shoes off. She put her head on my shoulder, the way she used to on the bus home from school.

"Thanks for being in the photos, Mum."

Three years. First time I'd cried happy.

Somewhere on the drive home I worked out what that summer had really been about.

For thirty years I took care of everybody. Then my body slowed down, and the man I'd taken care of told me I'd stopped taking care of myself.

And the worst part is, I half believed him.

I wasn't past it. My clock was running slow, and in 58 years nobody had ever told me why.

The week after, I went back on the EverCalm site. They're £39.99, and right now every ring comes with a second one free. So I ordered two, which meant four.

1 for Sue.

1 for Pauline, who wrote her email on the back of a place card.

1 for Jake's mum, who'd seen me in Cornwall and said she wanted whatever I was having.

And 1 for Kayleigh's mum. Kayleigh drove it round to her herself.

You get 90 days, and if you feel nothing, you send it back for every penny. My first week did nothing, so I wouldn't judge yours on the first week. Give it the month.

I don't know who's told you you've stopped taking care of yourself.

I only know that when somebody told me, it wasn't my age. It was one clock, running slow, that nobody had ever bothered to check.

I didn't go to that wedding to embarrass him. I gave him his ring back, and I stood next to him for Emma's photo.

I went because I'd spent three years at the back of every room, and I wasn't going to spend my daughter's wedding there too.

If somebody's already decided the back is where you belong, take the front row.
